tldr: The authors built a massive 1,500-hour bimanual household manipulation dataset and trained XR-2, a 5B VLA model. They demonstrated that performance plateaus from adding expert data can be broken by incorporating human on-policy correction data (DAgger).
hero_caption: Overview of the two-stage full-parameter training of XR-2. After pre-training on offline real-robot expert demonstrations (Stage 1), post-training (Stage 2) mixes in human-intervened correction trajectories (DAgger) collected from failure states during real deployment, bridging the policy's own distributional shift.
overview:
Bimanual household manipulation, such as folding laundry or operating washing machines, presents difficult challenges requiring coordinated dual-arm motion and long-horizon execution. While expectations for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have surged, the scarcity of high-quality bimanual real-robot demonstration data remains a major bottleneck. Furthermore, as data collection expands, a fundamental question about data scaling emerges: is it sufficient to merely keep gathering expert successes, or do we fundamentally need recovery data from failures?

To tackle this challenge, the authors constructed a massive 1,500-hour dataset combining mobile bimanual teleoperation on real robots (531.7 hours, 32,518 trajectories) and handheld UMI data collected in real homes (around 1,000 hours). They then proposed XR-2, a 5B-parameter VLA model pairing a multimodal foundation model (Qwen3-VL-4B) with a Flow Matching-based Action Expert. Following offline training, they integrated a DAgger pipeline where humans intervene and correct robot failures in real time during autonomous execution.

Evaluating data scaling on a real-robot garment folding task revealed that while expert data steadily boosted success rates from 10 to 120 hours (34% to 84%), it plateaued at 82% at 160 hours. In contrast, remedying the remaining failures with DAgger intervention data propelled the success rate from 58% up to 93% over three rounds. This highlights a crucial, highly practical scaling principle: once expert data covers the base distribution, on-policy correction data targeting real-world deployment failures becomes indispensable.
contributions: Released a 1,500-hour household bimanual manipulation dataset combining 531.7 hours of real bimanual robot teleoperation with approximately 1,000 hours of handheld UMI data gathered across more than 200 real homes.
Developed XR-2, a 5B-parameter bimanual VLA model combining Qwen3-VL-4B with a Flow Matching Action Expert, featuring Action Prefix conditioning for asynchronous real-time inference.
Constructed an on-policy DAgger loop that automatically extracts human failure-correction trajectories during real deployment, introducing a data mixing scheme that weights underperforming subtasks.

Demonstrated complementary scaling behavior on garment folding: while scaling expert demonstrations saturates around 120 hours, DAgger post-training dramatically elevates success rate from 58% to 93%.

sections.heading: A 25-DoF Whole-Body Robot and a 1,500-Hour Hybrid Collection Pipeline
sections.summary: This section details the hardware of the 'X2W' mobile bimanual robot and its 1,500-hour data collection pipeline. It combines offline VR teleoperated demonstrations, deployment-time DAgger corrections, and handheld UMI recordings in real homes.
sections.details:
### II-A Robot Platform
The experimental platform uses the "X2W" mobile bimanual robot, developed for whole-body coordinated manipulation. It features 25 degrees of freedom in total: two 7-DoF arms, two 1-DoF grippers, a 4-DoF waist, a 2-DoF neck, and a 3-wheeled omnidirectional base. All joints are driven by quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators offering high responsiveness and compliance.
The robot's proprioceptive state is an 89-dimensional vector integrating joint/wheel positions, velocities, torques, and end-effector poses. The control command is 25-dimensional, covering target positions for 22 joints and target velocities for the 3 wheels. Visual sensors include a head camera for broad scene context and two wrist cameras capturing fine-grained manipulation, all recorded synchronously at 30Hz.

### II-B Data Collection Pipeline
Data collection proceeds through two tracks: offline expert demonstrations and on-policy DAgger corrections. Long-horizon tasks are broken into natural subtasks, with standardized operating procedures (SOPs) specifying environments and initial configurations. Operators teleoperate via VR headsets. Demonstrations undergo cloud-based automated validation, VLM annotation, and visual inspection to ensure high quality.
In on-policy DAgger, whenever the autonomously operating robot fails or gets stuck, a human operator immediately takes over, recovers the subtask, and returns control. Without resetting the entire task, the intervention segment is logged as a correction demonstration, enabling a closed-loop improvement cycle without re-annotation.

### II-C Robot Dataset Overview
The real-robot dataset comprises 32,518 trajectories, 57.4M frames, and 531.7 hours. Workspace environments span four scenes: folding table (14.6k), washing machine (8.4k), sofa (6.1k), and laundry basket (3.4k). Episode lengths range from brief primitives to long-horizon tasks exceeding 150 seconds, labeled with 11 unified atomic skills (e.g., fold garment, load washer, lift basket).

### II-D UMI Dataset Overview
To enrich environmental diversity beyond stationary setups, the authors collected ~1,000 hours of garment manipulation using handheld grippers (UMI). Recorded by over 100 collectors across 200+ real homes, it covers more than 5,000 garments across beds, tables, and drying racks. The passive, vision-only gripper lacks encoders or motors, keeping it lightweight enough for continuous sessions up to 90 minutes without operator fatigue.

sections.heading: The 5B Foundation Architecture of XR-2 and Deficit-Targeted Data Mixing
sections.summary: This section explains XR-2, a 5B model combining a vision-language backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B) with a Flow Matching Action Expert. It introduces Action Prefix conditioning for low-latency asynchronous control, alongside a weighting algorithm to boost weak subtasks without catastrophic forgetting.
sections.details:
### III-A Main Architecture
XR-2 is a 5B-parameter VLA model combining Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for multimodal perception and a Transformer-based Action Expert for action generation. The Action Expert features hidden dimension 1024, 8 attention heads, and 18 blocks. Within each block, noisy action tokens undergo self-attention before performing Depth-aligned Cross-Attention into the VLM's corresponding intermediate layers. This aligns concrete early-layer visual representations up to abstract late-layer linguistic features directly with actions.
Furthermore, the model adopts "Action Prefix conditioning" for low-latency asynchronous control on real hardware. Actions corresponding to execution delay steps $d$ caused by inference latency are fixed as a deterministic prefix; noise injection and denoising are applied only to the remaining suffix. During inference, 5-step Euler integration provides extremely smooth real-time trajectory generation.

### III-B Expert Post-Training
Using the collected expert trajectories, multitask learning is conducted via a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) objective. Conditioned on robot observations, proprioception, and language instructions, the model learns a vector field mapping Gaussian noise to target action chunks.

### III-C DAgger Post-Training and Mixing Design
When integrating correction data from deployments, the training recipe must prevent catastrophic forgetting while effectively remediating weak tasks. The authors implement two key strategies. First, expert and DAgger data are mixed 1:1 based on trajectory count rather than frame count, preventing longer tasks from diluting shorter skills. Second, data is weighted based on subtask success rate $s_i$. The allocation ratio $w_i$ is computed as $w_i = w_{\min} + (1 - N w_{\min}) \frac{(1 - s_i + \epsilon)^\alpha}{\sum_j (1 - s_j + \epsilon)^\alpha}$ (with $w_{\min}=0.05, \epsilon=0.05, \alpha=1$). This balances forgetting prevention via a baseline quota $w_{\min}$ while focusing correction data on high-failure subtasks.

sections.heading: Expert Data Saturation and a Leap to 93% with DAgger
sections.summary: The authors built an asynchronous real-robot deployment environment on an RTX 4090 to quantitatively benchmark data scale against task performance on garment folding. They show that after expert scaling plateaus, DAgger training drives success rates from 58% to 93%.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The trained policy executes asynchronous inference at 10Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, predicting 50-step $\times$ 25-variable action chunks. Following Temporal Ensembling, whole-body joint commands are published at 30Hz and tracked by a low-level whole-body controller optimizing at 1,000Hz. The evaluation setup introduces deliberate generalization variations in garment sizes, colors, and initial robot poses; reaching an 85% success rate under these variations corresponds to over 95% under in-distribution conditions.

### IV-B Scaling Limits of Expert Demonstrations
Focusing on garment folding, the authors scaled training demonstrations from 10 to 160 hours (8,000 trajectories). Success rates scaled cleanly from 34% at 30 hours to 84% at 120 hours. However, performance plateaued at 82% with 160 hours; the extra 40 hours brought no improvement. This indicates state-space saturation for expert trajectories. Because subtle deployment drifts and failure states never occur in expert demonstrations, purely collecting more offline data hits an insurmountable out-of-distribution barrier.

### IV-C Performance Leap via DAgger Post-Training
To break this plateau, the authors applied the proposed DAgger post-training recipe to a base checkpoint trained on 10 subtasks and 18,695 trajectories (58% initial folding success). Fine-tuning for 2.5 epochs per round resulted in monotonic gains: 74% in round 1, 82% in round 2, and 93% in round 3. This 35-percentage-point surge over the expert-only baseline confirms that on-policy correction data is the decisive factor in overcoming offline demonstration saturation.

captions.F5: Scaling behaviors on garment folding: (a) success rate as a function of expert demonstration data, saturating around 120 hours (84%); (b) progression over 3 rounds of DAgger starting from a 58% checkpoint, consistently climbing to 93% via targeted correction data.

sections.heading: Diverse Household Tasks and In-the-Wild UMI Demonstrations
sections.summary: Visualizations of representative trajectories in the public dataset, highlighting real-robot manipulation tasks like washing machine operation and basket transport, alongside rich in-the-wild garment interactions recorded in private homes.
sections.details:
### Diverse Real-Robot Task Executions
Representative head-camera trajectories capture complex bimanual workflows: opening and closing washer doors, lifting and lowering laundry baskets with both arms, inserting plush toys into machines, moving garments onto a sofa, and long-horizon sequence unfolding and folding fabrics. Each phase is annotated with clean subtask instructions, structuring extended household routines into cohesive steps.

### In-The-Wild Home Data via UMI
Wrist-mounted UMI sequences depict interactions with a wide array of clothing, including red and white shirts, patterned sweaters, jackets, and jeans. Annotations capture fine-grained action steps at each midpoint—such as "fold sleeve first," "smooth wrinkles," and "stack garments." The collection vividly showcases the visual diversity across lighting, backgrounds, and textiles sourced from over 200 real homes.

captions.F7: Handheld UMI garment folding trajectories recorded in real households, capturing fine-grained steps (smoothing wrinkles, folding sleeves, stacking) across diverse home environments and lighting conditions.

takeaways: Scaling offline expert demonstrations faces an upper bound (saturating around 120 hours in this setting); continuing past this plateau requires on-policy interventions (DAgger) that visit the policy's own failure states.

When post-training with DAgger, mixing expert and correction data 1:1 by trajectory count and weighting sampling toward lower-performing subtasks prevents forgetting while efficiently instilling recovery behaviors.

A hybrid data collection paradigm combining lab-based robot teleoperation (530 hours) with handheld UMI recordings in real homes (1,000 hours) offers a highly effective strategy to capture diversity in bimanual manipulation.
limitations: Quantitative scaling laws were primarily evaluated on garment folding success rates; scaling limits and dynamics across other contact-rich tasks (e.g., washer operation) remain unverified.
On-policy DAgger collection still relies on real-time human monitoring and VR intervention, meaning it is not yet a fully autonomous self-improvement loop.
